text: Before a circuit ever touches a backend, you can verify a great deal about it: qubit count, gate sequence, parameter wiring, and decomposition structure. These checks are ordinary deterministic unit tests, and they should make up the majority of a quantum test suite — they're fast, they never flake, and they catch the most common class of real bugs.

This lesson covers inspecting a QuantumCircuit's internal structure without running it, patterns for testing parameterized circuits, how to test a decomposition or transpilation step deterministically, using pytest's parametrize to test a circuit-building function across many inputs efficiently, and why these tests should run in CI on every single commit.

A QuantumCircuit object exposes its gate sequence and qubit count directly through its data attribute — a list of instructions, each with a gate name and the qubits it acts on. A test like this one builds a four-qubit GHZ circuit, checks the qubit count, checks the exact gate-name sequence, and checks that every CX gate's control is qubit zero. This runs in milliseconds, needs no simulator or hardware, and will catch a real class of bugs: an off-by-one in a loop, a CX applied with qubits swapped, a missing Hadamard.

When a circuit gets transpiled to a backend's native gate set, the output depth and gate count are deterministic for a fixed transpiler seed and optimization level, which means they're testable. Notice the fixed seed_transpiler value here — without pinning it, optimization level one and above can use randomized heuristics for qubit layout, making depth vary between otherwise-identical runs. Pinning the seed here is the same reproducibility principle Chapter 4 covers for whole experiments, just applied to a single test.

pytest's parametrize marker lets one test function cover many circuit sizes without duplicating code. This is especially valuable for construction tests, because a bug like an off-by-one in a loop range often only appears at specific sizes — testing just n equals two tells you much less than testing two, three, five, and eight all from one test function.

Construction tests have no backend dependency, no network call, and no randomness once seeds are pinned, which means they should run on every single commit in CI, typically in well under a second for a whole suite. Statistical tests, which lesson seven builds, are slower and need a shot budget, so many teams run construction tests on every push and reserve statistical tests for merges to a main branch or a nightly job.
Next lesson builds the statistical-testing toolkit this chapter has been pointing toward — a calculated, justified pass-fail threshold for measurement outcomes, instead of a guess.
